e.t: Angai, also given as Angge, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). Its meaning is not an ordinary descriptive idea such as an action, quality, or object; it functions as a specific name. The form occurs four times in this corpus, in Genesis 12:8, Genesis 13:3, and Isaiah 10:28–29. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be identified more specifically here.

This adjective means "unknown": something not known, recognized, or familiar. It describes a person, thing, or matter whose identity or nature has not been discovered or understood. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on the absence of knowledge or recognition; the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is unknown in each use.

Adiel is a personal name, also rendered Athil. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 9:12. The available lexical information preserves the name forms but does not provide a further descriptive meaning, so its ordinary sense is simply the person’s name. The exact significance of that individual in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Azeni is a proper name used to identify someone or something named Azeni. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Numbers 26:25. The available wording gives the name itself but does not provide a separate descriptive meaning or explain whether it identifies a person, family, or another named group. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Ailōth, also rendered Eloth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. It identifies a named person, place, or other entity in the biblical account, but the supplied material does not include enough verse text to specify which kind of entity it names. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Kings 14:22. Its precise significance there must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage.

This noun means “accuracy”: careful exactness or correctness in what is known, said, or done. It describes attention to things as they truly are rather than carelessness or approximation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times—once in Daniel and three times in Wisdom and Sirach—so it is a relatively uncommon word. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains careful correctness and exactness.

This noun refers to a sea-eagle or osprey, a bird identified by name in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs twice in the Septuagint, once in Leviticus and once in Deuteronomy, in lists of birds. The wording points to the bird itself rather than to an action or quality. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding list and verse context.

Alloni is a personal name, rendered “Allōni” or “Alloni.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Numbers 26:22. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name itself does not provide further information about the person or the role he has in that passage. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name Alloni.

This noun means “vine worker”: a person who works with grapevines, especially by tending or cultivating a vineyard. It names an occupation rather than a place, tool, or abstract quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, showing a focused term for people engaged in vineyard labor. Its exact action in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but the word itself identifies the worker by the kind of work performed.

“Lawlessly” describes an action done without regard for law or lawful order. As an adverb, it tells how someone acts rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 8:17. Its basic sense is clear from the direct definition, while the surrounding verse determines the specific action or situation being described there.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “controversy,” referring to a matter of dispute between parties. It names the disagreement itself rather than an action or a person. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 19 verses, showing that it is used repeatedly for contested matters. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “demanding back”—the act of requiring something to be returned or repaid. It describes a claim made to recover what is owed, rather than simply asking for something for the first time. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages in Nehemiah, Zephaniah, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being demanded and the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “drive away”: to cause someone or something to leave or be sent away. It describes an action of removing or forcing away rather than simply noticing departure. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, appearing once each in 1 Samuel, Ezekiel, and Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding passage says is being driven away.

This Greek LXX verb means “wash off”: it describes removing something by washing it away. It is an action word, focusing on cleansing or getting something off rather than simply becoming clean. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in 1 Kings 22:38 and Proverbs 30:12, 20. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This verb means “fall from”: to move downward away from a place, position, or source. It describes separation through falling rather than simply being low or falling in place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages from Leviticus, Job, and Psalms. The exact object or circumstance involved depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains a falling away or down from something.

This word is a proper name: “Arkesaios” or “Arkeseos.” It identifies a person bearing that name in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once in the LXX, at Esther 1:14. Since no verse text or surrounding passage is available here, the name itself does not support a broader meaning such as a character trait, action, or spiritual theme. Its role in that verse must be understood from the passage’s actual context.

gl: that by which anything is carried; device for carrying building material
d: that by which anything is carried; device for carrying building material

e.t: This noun refers to a means of carrying something, especially a device used to transport building material. It names an object rather than an action or a person, so its basic sense is practical and concrete: equipment that bears or conveys materials. The word therefore points to a tool or implement for moving supplies, not to the supplies themselves. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 4:11.

This adverb means acting “honourably; honestly”—in a way marked by integrity, proper conduct, and truthfulness. It describes how someone carries out an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:43. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is conduct that is upright and sincere.

This noun means “tale” or “narrative,” referring to a communicated account or story. It names the account itself rather than an action or quality. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs only once, in 4 Maccabees 14:6. The surrounding verse text is not included, so the word’s precise role in that passage cannot be described further; its central meaning remains an account or story.

This Greek LXX noun means “acorn,” the nut produced by an oak tree. It names a small, familiar part of the natural world rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing across Genesis, Judges, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary meaning remains the oak’s seed or nut.

“Bamōthbaal” or “Vamothvaal” is a proper name, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 13:17. The available information identifies the name and its two listed forms, but does not provide the verse text or a broader set of uses. Therefore, its precise significance beyond functioning as a named designation cannot be stated here.

This word refers to a kind of serpent, commonly rendered “basilisk.” It can function as a noun for the creature itself or as an adjective describing something associated with such a serpent. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Psalms 90:13 and once in Isaiah 59:5. The word identifies a particular serpent rather than expressing a general term for every snake; its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “help”—assistance given to someone in need or difficulty. It names the aid a person receives or provides, rather than an action by itself. The word appears 62 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing a broad use for needed support. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Ganēbath, also rendered Ganivath, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Septuagint, it refers to a named individual and occurs twice in one verse, 1 Kings 11:20. The available passage information preserves the name but not the surrounding verse text, so it gives no further meaning beyond identifying the person by name. The two forms represent this same proper name.

“Earthborn” describes a person or thing as born from the earth or belonging to earthly life. It is an adjective, so it characterizes someone or something rather than naming an action. This Greek LXX word occurs five times, in Psalms, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a description of earthly birth or origin.

e.h: A Creature with a Rough Foot
e.t: This noun refers to a creature identified as “rough-foot.” In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only twice, once in Leviticus 11:5 and once in Deuteronomy 14:7. Its wording describes the creature by a notable physical feature rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. The precise significance of the term in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense remains a creature characterized by a rough foot.

Deberi is a proper name, referring to a specific person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered as “Deberi” and is also identified as “Theveri.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:57. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be described further; its supported lexical function is simply a personal name.

This noun means “warden,” referring to a person responsible for guarding prisoners or overseeing a prison. It identifies an official whose duty is connected with custody and supervision, rather than describing a prisoner or a place. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Genesis 40:3. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a prison warden or keeper.

“Penetrate” means to enter through or pass into something. As a verb, this word describes an action of breaking through or making one’s way into a place or barrier. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Numbers 14:44. The word’s basic sense remains focused on entry by passing through, while the precise force of that action in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This noun means “covenant,” referring to an established commitment or agreement between parties. It names a relationship formed by an acknowledged obligation, rather than merely a casual promise. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 337 times, showing that covenant language is a substantial and recurring part of this corpus. Its earliest recorded occurrence is Genesis 6:18, and the term continues through 2 Maccabees 8:15.

This verb means “disperse” or “confound”: to scatter something or someone so that unity, order, or shared purpose is broken. It can describe people being driven apart, or a situation being thrown into confusion. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 49 times, chiefly in Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Psalms, showing that it is used repeatedly for scattering and confusing. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being dispersed or confounded and on the surrounding sentence.

This verb means to “overturn utterly,” expressing the complete overthrow or ruin of something rather than a minor change. As a verb, it describes an action that leaves what was established decisively brought down. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 5:12. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being overturned there, but the word itself points to thorough and decisive overthrow.

This verb means “dawn”: it describes day beginning as morning light appears. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used four times, each in a different verse, to express the arrival of dawn or the passing from night toward daylight. Its basic sense is temporal and descriptive, pointing to the beginning of the day rather than to a person, object, or action performed by someone. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

This word means “right” or “just.” As an adjective or noun, it describes someone or something regarded as right, just, or belonging to what is right. It can characterize people, conduct, or a standing that accords with what is proper. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it appears 370 times, showing that this is a broad and regularly used description rather than a rare expression. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “in hard labor,” describing someone undergoing difficult labor, especially the strenuous work of childbirth. It is a verb, so it expresses an action or condition rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Genesis 35:16. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is labor marked by difficulty or distress.

This noun means a “dagger” or “handknife,” referring to a small handheld blade. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, in six verses, including passages in Exodus, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its basic meaning remains concrete and practical: a short knife or dagger used as an implement or weapon. The surrounding verse determines the particular use, but the word itself points to the blade rather than to an action or abstract idea.

gl: father of the nation; father of our nation
d: father of the nation; father of our nation

e.t: This noun means “father of the nation” or “father of our nation.” It describes a person viewed as the paternal founder, ancestor, or honored father of a people. The wording can express national identity and respect, rather than merely referring to someone’s role as a biological parent. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 16:20; the surrounding verse is needed to determine its precise force there.

This adjective means “hundredfold”: something multiplied or increased by a hundred. It describes the degree or amount of something rather than naming an object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 2 Samuel 24:3 and once in 1 Chronicles 21:3. Those references identify its two occurrences, while the surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is described as hundredfold in each passage.

This verb means to “deviate” or “avoid”—to turn aside from a direction, path, or course, or to keep away from something. It describes an action rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, it occurs 146 times, so it is used broadly for turning away or avoiding. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on what is being approached, left, or avoided there.

This Greek LXX verb means “angry; incensed,” describing a person who has become strongly angered. It expresses an active emotional response rather than a calm judgment or mild displeasure. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 3:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is clear: to become deeply angry or stirred with indignation.

e.h: Make Less or Be in Need
e.t: This Greek Old Testament verb means “make less” or describes being “in need.” It expresses reduction—making something smaller, fewer, or diminished—or a condition in which something is lacking. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis and Psalms. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being reduced or what kind of need the surrounding passage describes.

This Greek LXX verb means “abide”: to remain, continue, or stay faithful to a person, place, condition, or stated commitment. It presents abiding as an ongoing action rather than a momentary stay. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, so its basic sense applies across several kinds of statements. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains continuing or standing by.

“Spout” describes an action that sends something outward. It functions as a verb, focusing on the act itself rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs only once, in Wisdom 15:11. Its central sense is therefore a forceful outward release, while the exact thing being released must be understood from the surrounding verse. This is a rare word in this corpus and should not be broadened into a general term for every kind of speaking, flowing, or expressing.

This word means “six hundredth,” identifying something by its position as number 600 in an ordered sequence. It is an adjective, so it describes a person, thing, or time associated with that ordinal number rather than naming the number six hundred itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis, at Genesis 7:11 and Genesis 8:13. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being identified as six hundredth.

This Greek LXX verb means to fully explore—to search something out carefully and thoroughly rather than examine it only briefly. It describes deliberate investigation, whether the subject is a place, a situation, or something being sought. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, showing a repeated sense of thorough searching across different settings. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being investigated there.

This Greek LXX verb means “impose” or “cast on”: it describes putting something onto someone or something, or laying a matter upon them. Depending on the sentence, it can refer to placing a physical object, applying a burden, or assigning something. It occurs 66 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so its exact force is determined by the surrounding words. Its basic idea remains an action of putting or laying something upon another.

This noun means “victory over”—the achievement of prevailing against someone or something. It names an outcome in which one side gains mastery or triumph over another, rather than describing the act of fighting itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 8:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but the word’s central sense remains the successful overcoming of an opponent or opposing power.

This verb means “care for; take care of.” It describes giving someone or something attentive help, oversight, or practical concern. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming the person receiving care or the care itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs four times across Genesis, Proverbs, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any one passage comes from the surrounding sentence and situation.

This adjective describes someone or something as “notorious” or “notable”—recognized because of an unusual, important, or well-known quality. It can point to distinction that attracts attention, whether the recognition is favorable or unfavorable. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, functioning as a descriptive word rather than naming an action or object. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what person or thing it describes.

gl: that which is baked over the fire
d: that which is baked over the fire

e.t: This noun refers to something baked over a fire. It names a prepared food item rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 6:19. The word’s basic sense is specific and concrete: food made by baking over fire. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the verse’s wording.

gl: blessing of children; breed of goodly children
d: blessing of children; breed of goodly children

e.t: This noun refers to the blessing, prosperity, or good outcome connected with having children. It describes children as a gift and a source of family flourishing, rather than naming a specific child or describing the act of birth itself. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 18:9. Its central sense is expressed by “blessing of children” and “breed of goodly children.” The precise force of its single use depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Ērōn, rendered “Iron,” is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing a quality or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 7:61, within a list of people connected with the return from exile. Because the available text does not include the surrounding verse, the name itself gives no further personal description or significance. Its basic function is simply to identify this individual in that genealogical or community record.

Thana is a proper name, identifying a person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 1 Chronicles 4:12. The available information identifies the name itself but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain whom or what Thana designates in that passage. Its meaning is therefore best stated simply as the personal or place name “Thana,” with its specific reference determined by the context of 1 Chronicles 4:12.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Thēsous” or “Thisus.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Samuel 5:16. The available information establishes the name and its grammatical function, but the verse text is needed to explain which person bears it or what role that person has in the passage.

This adjective describes something as “hot” or “warm,” referring to its temperature. It can characterize an object, condition, or surrounding circumstance that has noticeable heat. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX corpus, it occurs nine times, showing a recurring but relatively focused use for describing warmth or heat. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central meaning remains a physical condition of being hot or warm.

This word is a proper name, rendered as “Ideia” or “Ithia.” It identifies a specific person or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 24:7. Because the available information gives only the name and reference—not the verse text or surrounding passage—the precise identity and role connected with it must be determined from that passage’s context.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Iebousai” or “Ievuse.” It identifies a specifically named person, people, or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 18:16. The name’s precise identification and significance depend on the surrounding passage, since the word itself functions primarily as a name rather than a descriptive term.

Ierkaan is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears twice, both occurrences being in the same verse of 1 Chronicles.2.44. The available lexical information identifies the word simply as “Ierkaan,” so its ordinary meaning is its function as a proper name. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the person and explain his specific place in that genealogy.

This Greek LXX noun means “inflammation; burning,” describing a hot, inflamed condition or the burning sensation associated with it. It is used in Old Testament passages concerning bodily inflammation, injury, and burning materials. The word occurs ten times in the Greek LXX, including five occurrences in Leviticus and two in Exodus. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains an inflamed or burning condition.

This verb means to “war down”: to overcome or wear down through sustained conflict. It describes an active effort against an opposing force rather than a peaceful disagreement or ordinary difficulty. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 10:25. Because the available wording gives the basic lexical sense but not the verse text, the precise force of the command or statement there depends on its surrounding passage.

This word means “down” or “below,” describing a lower position, direction, or place. It can function as an adverb, modifying an action by showing that it happens downward, or as a preposition, identifying something situated beneath or lower than another thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 25 times, primarily in the Old Testament portion of the Septuagint. Its basic idea remains focused on location or movement from a higher place toward a lower one. [evidence IDs: p03:word:lxx:L707557:identity; p03:word:lxx:L707557:occurrences]

Kisai, also rendered Kise, is a proper name identifying a person rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:29. The available meaning does not provide an additional definition beyond this personal name, so its significance is identifying the individual named in that genealogy. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s specific place in the passage.

This noun means “greave,” a piece of protective armor worn over the lower leg. It refers to equipment used as part of a warrior’s armor rather than to a person, action, or inner quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Samuel 17:6. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies a protective covering for the leg.

This adjective means “pastoral,” describing something connected with caring for or tending herds. It is used in the Greek Old Testament to identify people or a way of life associated with livestock and their care. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis and Numbers. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the pastoral life and work of tending animals.

This word means “gluttony,” referring to excessive or uncontrolled eating. It is a noun that names an appetite or behavior rather than describing a person, object, or action in general. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 1:27. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its central meaning remains the indulgence of food beyond proper restraint.

This noun means “declaration.” It refers to something declared and functions as a naming word, rather than describing an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 35 times, with most occurrences in Psalms. It appears in Numbers, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Isaiah, and Wisdom, showing use across several biblical books. The precise force of any occurrence is determined by its surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a pestilent condition—a state marked by disease or pestilence. It names the condition itself rather than describing a person, action, or object affected by it. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Esther 8:12. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a harmful, disease-bearing condition.

Mal is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, in 1 Kings 5:11. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its particular role in that verse cannot be described further. The name itself carries no broader ordinary meaning beyond identifying the person called Mal.

Manios is a personal name, referring to a man named Manios rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. It functions as a proper name in the Greek LXX corpus. The name occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 11:34. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the person’s role or significance in that passage cannot be stated from the name alone.

Maseron is a proper name, referring to a specific person or place rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in Joshua 11:8, and is rendered “Maseron.” Because it is a name, its meaning is mainly its identifying function: it distinguishes the particular person or location named in that passage. The available information does not provide an additional ordinary definition or describe the named entity beyond this identification.

This word means “black,” describing a dark color or appearance. As an adjective, it identifies something by its visible darkness rather than naming an object or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, including descriptions associated with people, hair, and horses. Its basic meaning remains consistent across these uses: something is black or dark in appearance. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being described, but the word itself supplies the color distinction.

This Greek LXX verb means “draw up; furl,” describing the action of pulling something upward or folding it into a compact form. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in Proverbs 31:13. Its basic sense identifies an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being drawn up or furled there.

This noun means “one who rules alone; monarch”—a single person who holds supreme authority as ruler. It describes the ruler himself rather than the act of ruling. In the Greek LXX material represented here, the word occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 2:2. The English rendering at that occurrence does not by itself express the full lexical meaning, so the central idea remains the identity of a sole or absolute ruler. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “molar,” a tooth used for grinding food. It names a specific kind of tooth rather than a general reference to the mouth or to teeth as a whole. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament portion represented here, appearing once each in Job, Psalms, Proverbs, and Joel. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a molar tooth.

Nachor is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It refers to the man named Nachor rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name appears 19 times in this LXX corpus, across 18 verses, with most occurrences in Genesis. Its meaning is therefore primarily personal identification: when readers encounter Nachor, they are being told which individual is named. The spelling “Nakhor” is another rendering of the same name.

This adjective refers to “legalities”—matters connected with what is legally required or established. It describes something understood in relation to law, rather than naming a person, action, or place. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, it occurs 72 times, showing a recurring concern with matters governed by authorized requirements. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the noun or situation it describes.

This Greek LXX noun means “way” or “journey”: a path or route that someone travels. It can describe movement from one place to another, whether understood as the road itself or the journey along it. The word is broadly used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, occurring 676 times, so its precise sense in a particular verse depends on how the surrounding sentence presents the way or journey.

Orech is a proper name, rendered as “Orech” in English. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word with a broader definition, so its meaning is chiefly its role as the name of a particular person, place, or family designation in the Old Testament text. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: in Genesis 10:10 and 1 Chronicles 7:39. The surrounding verse text would be needed to identify exactly what Orech names in each passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to make something fast and sure, or to fortify it. It describes strengthening a person, place, or structure so that it becomes secure and able to withstand opposition. The idea is active: something is made firm rather than merely found in a firm condition. This word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Joshua, Chronicles, Jeremiah, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being strengthened and the surrounding context.

This adjective describes something done or present “with the whole multitude”—that is, together with an entire gathered crowd or community. It emphasizes the participation of everyone in the group rather than a small part of it. In the Greek LXX, this word appears once, in 2 Maccabees 10:24. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense points to collective involvement by the whole assembled multitude.

Parosom is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament text rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 1 Chronicles 23:7. The available lexical information identifies it only as “Parosōm; Parosom,” so its meaning is the personal name itself. The surrounding verse context would be needed to explain the person’s role in that passage.

This adjective describes a neighbor or something connected with a neighboring area. It can refer to nearby people, a surrounding district, or what belongs to that neighborhood. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs nine times, so its basic sense is consistent but its precise force depends on the sentence where it appears. The word is used across several Old Testament books, including Genesis, Deuteronomy, Judges, 1 Kings, and Jeremiah.

This Greek LXX adverb means “variously,” describing something done or occurring in different ways. It modifies an action or statement by showing variety rather than one uniform manner.
